definition: Secularization is the process by which religion loses its authority over a society's institutions and daily life — schools, laws, and customs passing from religious into worldly hands.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word secularization. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know secularization should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The village charted its own secularization in the parish ledger: weddings moved to the town hall, the school dropped morning prayers, and the saint's day became a farmers' market.

Disestablishment is milder than secularization: one statute cuts the church's official state status, while the pews, schools, and customs may go on exactly as before — secularization is the deeper current that empties religion's authority from all of them.

Desacralization goes further than secularization — secularization moves institutions out of religion's control, while desacralization drains the very sense of the sacred from a culture, until nothing at all is set apart as holy.

Disestablishment is a single legal act — a church losing its official status as the state's church, one tie cut by statute. Secularization is the far wider drift such an act may belong to: schools, courts, holidays, and habits passing one by one out of religion's orbit.

Laicization hands an institution's controls from clergy to laypeople — a lay principal, a civilian board — and it can happen while the place stays devout. Secularization goes to the root: it removes religion's authority itself, not just the collars from the committee.

Secular is the adjective underneath: a secular state, secular music, a secular age — belonging to this present world rather than to any religious frame. Latin saeculum built almost nothing else in English, so this small family keeps its root to itself.
Secularization is the process by which religion loses its authority over a society's institutions and daily life — schools, laws, and customs passing from religious into worldly hands.

The secularization of Aldercroft College took a century and left fingerprints on every charter revision: chapel became optional in the 1920s, the divinity requirement shrank to an elective in the 1960s, and when the last chaplain retired, the mission statement was quietly reworded to speak of 'service' where it had once said 'salvation.'

Secularization is the precise word for that long transfer, because it names the process by which institutions pass out of religion's control and into worldly hands — not an attack on belief, but a slow migration of authority.
The chapel still stands at Aldercroft; what changed is that nothing at the college answers to it anymore.
Secularization is a historian's process word: it takes decades, and its object is institutions and public life, not private belief — a person can pray daily inside a thoroughly secularized state.

Keep its neighbors straight: disestablishment is one legal cut; laicization changes who runs an institution; and modernization swaps old for new on any axis at all — plumbing, dress, management — and by itself says nothing about religion.

A chapter in our comparative-history reader follows one small alpine republic through its public records from 1850 to 1950.
In 1850, the church ran the schools, licensed the printers, and set the calendar of workdays and rest days.

The secularization that followed was not one dramatic law but a hundred small transfers: teachers' exams moved to a state office, printing licenses to a civil registry, holidays to a parliamentary vote.
Church attendance, the author notes, barely changed across the century — the pews were as full in 1950 as in 1850.
What changed was authority: decisions that had once needed a bishop's signature now needed a clerk's stamp.
